## The question {#sec-question}

The Thistle is a 17 ft (5.2 m) one-design dinghy. Its centreboard has an 18 in (457 mm) chord. It
hangs from rollers on top of the trunk, at whatever angle it naturally takes, and reaches about
4 ft below the hull (an estimate from the class's draft). Which section shape gives it the least
drag?

The class rules [@tca-rules-2026] set two limits that matter here:

* **Thickness.** A board may be at most **1 in** thick overall (Article XII.5): 5.56\ % of the chord.
  Every section on this page is exactly 1 in thick.
* **Shape.** Every board "must meet the dimensions and shape as shown on the Official Plans"
  (XII.2). The plans are not online, so whether they fix the section is not known. **Check with a
  class measurer before building a board.**

The board stays fully down on every leg. Upwind runs from 0 to 5 knots of boat speed, downwind up
to 15 knots. No published section for the Thistle's board was found, so the study chose
**NACA 0006 scaled to 1 in**, the simplest standard section of that thickness, as its reference.

**The rule for ranking**, agreed before the simulations:

1. **Upwind first:** the board's drag at the same side force, over the upwind speeds.
2. **Stall margin:** a section must keep at least 2° between the high upwind load and its
   maximum side force, and not be more than 1° worse than NACA 0006.
3. **Downwind as tie-break or veto:** within ±1\ % upwind, the downwind drag decides. A section that
   loses more downwind than it gains upwind is vetoed.

## The board and the flow {#sec-board}

**Terms used on this page.**

* **Chord and section.** The chord is the board's width measured square to its leading edge, 18 in.
  The section is the shape of the board cut along that chord.
* **Side force and lift.** The side force $S_h$ is the whole board's force across the boat, in
  newtons, that stops it sliding sideways. The lift coefficient $C_l$ is the same thing for the
  section alone, made dimensionless.
* **Leeway and section angle.** Leeway $β_Y$ is the angle between where the boat points and where it
  goes (top view). The section angle $α_n$ is the angle at which the water meets the section, square
  to the raked edge: slightly more than the leeway.
* **Rake** $Λ$ is the fore-and-aft tilt of the board's leading edge from vertical (side view). It is not
  leeway.
* **Reynolds number** Re is speed × chord ÷ the water's viscosity. Here it runs from 0.23 to 3.5
  million, and it sets how the thin layer of water next to the board behaves.
* **Tu** is the turbulence intensity the simulation feeds in at its inlet. On this page it is a model
  input calibrated against a wind tunnel (@sec-calibration), not a measurement of lake water.

::: {layout-ncol=1}
![The board from the side: raked aft at an assumed 10°. The water meets the leading edge at an angle,
so its speed splits into a part square to the edge, $V_n$, which the section works with, and a smaller
part along it.](../_generated/thistle-board-side.svg){#fig-board-side width="520px"}

![The same boat from above (leeway exaggerated): the board makes side force across the water's
direction and drag along it. Leeway is this sideways angle; rake (above) is a fore-and-aft tilt.](../_generated/thistle-board-top.svg){#fig-board-top width="520px"}
:::

**The rake.** How far the board rakes when fully down is not published anywhere that was found. The
rules forbid making it hang more upright than it naturally does (XII.9). This study assumes **10°**
and checks 5° and 15°.

**Which chord does the water see?** Along the flow the chord is longer than 18 in: 18.07, 18.28 and
18.63 in at 5°, 10° and 15° of rake, through a section a little thinner than 5.56\ %. The study works
the other way round, with **simple sweep theory**: it simulates the board's own section, 18 in and
5.56\ %, in a flow of speed $V_n = V_b \cos Λ$, and maps the forces back to the whole board.

**What is compared.** The board's drag $D_h$ has two parts:

* **profile drag**, what the section itself makes: skin friction of the water rubbing along the
  surface, plus pressure drag from the wake behind it;
* **induced drag**, the cost of making side force with a board of finite depth. It is estimated from
  the side force with lifting-line theory, using an assumed span and efficiency.

Sections are compared at the **same side force**, the one the crew needs, and the section with the
lower **total** board drag wins. The CFD itself is 2D, one section in a plane. The board totals add the
sweep mapping and the assumed span and efficiency, the same for every section, so they shift the
absolute numbers more than the comparison.

**The loads.** The low, working and high side-force loads are the side forces NACA 0006 makes at 1°,
2° and 4° at each boat speed: at 5 knots about 200-220, 400-440 and 790 N. They are levels of side
force, not of wind. The working load matches a rough estimate from the crew's righting moment, about
440 N at 5 knots (an estimate, methodology-thistle.md §3).

**No race time.** The [IOM pages](../custom-section/) turn drag and leeway into race time with the
boat's resistance curve. There is no such curve for the Thistle, so drag and leeway are reported
separately here.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The formulas behind the board totals (click to open)

With $q = \tfrac12 \rho V_b^2$, $c$ the 18 in chord, $b$ = 1.24 m of board along the leading edge
(assumed), $e$ = 0.9 (assumed, with the hull acting as a mirror) and the section's lift, pressure-drag
and friction-drag coefficients $C_l$, $C_{d,p}$, $C_{d,f}$ from the CFD at $V_n$:

$$
S_h = C_l\, q \cos^2\!Λ\; c\, b
$$

$$
D_v = \left(C_{d,p} \cos^3\!Λ + C_{d,f} \cos Λ\right) q\, c\, b
$$

$$
D_i = \frac{S_h^2}{2\pi\, q\, e\, (b \cos Λ)^2}
$$

$D_h = D_v + D_i$, and the leeway is $β_Y = α_n \cos Λ$. Every simulated point is used again for any
rake; @sec-rake shows how much the rake moves the comparison.
:::

![Every simulated point: boat speed against section angle. Upwind speeds run 0-10°, downwind speeds
0-2°. The diamonds are the screen of all eight sections; the circles are the finalists' full grid. The
dotted lines are the three side-force loads. Reynolds number on the 18 in chord at $V_n$, fresh water at
20 °C.](../_generated/thistle-grid.svg){#fig-grid width="560px"}

At 0.23 to 3.5 million the Reynolds number is 3 to 30 times higher than on an IOM fin. The layer of
water next to a smooth section can stay smooth (laminar) over much of the chord, and where it turns
turbulent decides much of the drag.

## The sections {#sec-sections}

![The eight sections of the CFD screen at true scale: 1 in thick on an 18 in chord, leading edge (LE)
on the left. The tick marks the thickest point; on the two parallel-sided boards, the two ends of the
flat. Drawn from the coordinates used for the simulations.](../_generated/thistle-shapes.svg){#fig-shapes width="560px"}

![The same sections with the thickness stretched, so the differences show: the smooth sections, the
parallel-sided boards, and four of them minus NACA 0006.](../_generated/thistle-profiles.svg){#fig-profiles width="560px"}

![The noses at true scale, the first 1.2 in of the chord. Line styles as above.](../_generated/thistle-noses.svg){#fig-noses width="560px"}

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-properties}
{{< include ../_generated/thistle-properties.md >}}

The eight sections at 1 in on 18 in. Positions are from the leading edge. Nose radius and
trailing-edge angle are estimates from the coordinates (the angle from the last 0.5\ % of the chord).
:::

* **NACA 0006** is the reference: the NACA 4-digit section, thickest at 30\ % of the chord.
* **NACA 63-006 and 64-006** are laminar-flow sections from NACA Report 824 [@abbott1945]. They are
  thickest further back, which is meant to keep the boundary layer laminar for longer near zero lift.
  Their noses are sharper. The study fitted smooth shapes to the report's tables with the nose radius
  held, and scaled them from 6\ % to 5.56\ %.
* **NACA 0006-64** is NACA 0006 with its crest moved back to 40\ %: a smaller step the same way.
* **HT35** is Mark Drela's glider tail section, the [IOM fin study's](../custom-section/) winner, and
  **SD8020** a sharp-nosed low-speed section; both from the UIUC database [@uiuc-coords].
* **The two parallel-sided boards** are flat in the middle, as many home-built boards are. The
  **plank** is an assumed typical one: half-round nose, flat from 10\ % to 75\ % of the chord, and a
  straight taper. **parallel-l30-t50** is the best of 144 parallel-sided shapes in XFOIL, from the
  family of Saporito et al. [-@saporito2020]: long tapers and a flat only from 30\ % to 50\ %.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The XFOIL screen, selected sections (click to open)

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-xfoil}
{{< include ../_generated/thistle-xfoil.md >}}

XFOIL [@drela1989] estimates of ΔD, the board's drag against NACA 0006, %, rake 10°. Upwind: the mean
over 1-5 knots and the three side-force loads; downwind: 0° over 1-15 knots. "Tripped": transition
forced at 5\ % of the chord. XFOIL's turbulence is set through Ncrit (Mack's correlation). Negative =
less drag. The last column marks the eight sections that went on to the CFD. The parallel-sided row is
the best of the 144-shape family (no Tu 0.5\ % run).
:::

XFOIL under-predicts the drag of these sections at Re 3 million by 2-25\ % against Report 824, and
its maximum lift for them is unusable (0.26-1.08 depending on Ncrit, against 0.83 measured). So it
only chose which sections to simulate. Two things it showed that the CFD did not test: a 7/8 in NACA
0006 is about level upwind at Tu 1\ % and 3-5\ % better downwind, and a 3/4 in one loses upwind in
calm water. Thinner boards were outside the agreed scope.
:::

## How the answer was found {#sec-method}

![The steps of the study, from fast and rough to slow and careful: about 830 CFD cases in all.](../_generated/thistle-pipeline.svg){#fig-pipeline width="480px"}

### The simulations

The CFD is the project's 2D section model (`foil2d`): OpenFOAM [@openfoam], a steady solver, and the
k-ω SST turbulence model [@menter1994] with the Langtry-Menter transition model [@langtry2009], which
predicts where the boundary layer turns from laminar to turbulent. The section sits in a C-shaped mesh
50 chords across, with the first cell at the wall thin enough to resolve the laminar boundary layer
($y^+$ at most 2).

![The fine mesh around NACA 0006 at 18 in, from the same generator the runs use.](../_generated/thistle-mesh.png){#fig-mesh width="560px"}

**Which mesh, and how fine a difference it resolves.** Three sections on four meshes, 96 cases. The
fine mesh is within 2-3\ % of the extra-fine one in drag at most points, and up to about 7\ % where
the transition sits mid-chord at the working load. So **differences under about 3\ % between sections
are not resolved**. This is a resolution threshold from the mesh study, not a calibrated error bar.

![Drag on each mesh against the fine mesh, per test point, transition model at Tu 0.1\ %. The band is
±3\ %. The two large extra-fine departures on NACA 0006 are not mesh effects: one case stopped early
while its transition was still moving, the other settled into a different leading-edge bubble
(findings log).](../_generated/thistle-mesh-study.svg){#fig-mesh-study width="560px"}

### Checked against wind-tunnel data

NACA Report 824 [@abbott1945] measured NACA 0006 and 64-006, true 6\ % sections, at Re 3 million in a
low-turbulence wind tunnel: a Reynolds number the Thistle's board reaches only at about 13 knots. Both
were simulated at those conditions, 28 cases.

![Drag against lift from the simulations and from Report 824 (black). With the tunnel's own low
turbulence (green squares) the transition model gives too little drag at low lift; with a Tu input of
0.3\ % (red) it matches NACA 0006; 64-006 lies between 0.3 and 0.6\ % (orange). Fully turbulent
(purple) gives too much.](../_generated/thistle-validation-drag.svg){#fig-validation-drag width="560px"}

![Lift against angle: right below stall for both models. Hollow markers did not converge.](../_generated/thistle-validation-lift.svg){#fig-validation-lift width="560px"}

* **Lift is right below stall,** within about 0.03 in $C_l$ up to 6° for both sections and models.
* **At the tunnel's turbulence the model is too laminar at low lift:** its drag is 23-40\ % low at
  $C_l$ 0-0.2, and it keeps a laminar low-drag range on 64-006 at $C_l$ 0.2 that the measurements
  don't show. At $C_l$ 0.45-0.65 it is within 2\ %.
* **Fully turbulent is too draggy** at low lift, by 18-90\ %.
* **64-006 stalls early in the model:** maximum $C_l$ about 0.64 against 0.83 measured. NACA 0006,
  with its rounder nose, is right to 8°.

### Calibrating the turbulence input {#sec-calibration}

The transition model reads the incoming turbulence as one number, Tu. Which value makes it reproduce
the quiet tunnel? 40 more cases swept the input from 0.15 to 1.5\ % on the same two sections at 0-4°.

![Drag against Report 824 at the same $C_l$, for each angle, as the Tu input rises. The band is ±6\ %.
NACA 0006 matches at about 0.3\ %, 64-006 at about 0.45\ % (interpolated).](../_generated/thistle-calibration.svg){#fig-calibration width="560px"}

* **NACA 0006 matches at an input of 0.3\ %,** within ±6\ % at 0-4°; **64-006 at about 0.45\ %.**
* So at any one input the model gives 64-006 10-20\ % less drag, relative to its measurement, than it
  gives NACA 0006 at low lift: **the model favours the 6-series** by about that much.
* **At Re 3 million, inputs of 1\ % and above behave as fully turbulent:** the drag at 1 and 1.5\ % is
  the same. That was shown for these tunnel cases; it was not checked at the board's lower Reynolds
  numbers.

**What the input means, and what it does not.** The tunnel's real turbulence was a few hundredths of
a percent; 0.3-0.6\ % is what *this model* needs to reproduce it. So Tu here is a model setting, and
the calibrated 0.3-0.6\ % is a **bracket of inputs** inferred from one tunnel at one Reynolds number,
not a measured range for a calm lake and not a physical lower bound. A real board meets several
things this one number cannot represent separately: the water's own turbulence, the roughness of a
real board's surface, and waves that keep changing the angle. Tu 1\ % is used as a **higher-input
sensitivity case**, not as a conversion of rough water. Literature estimates of near-surface lake
turbulence [@remmlinger2013, not peer reviewed] are background only (docs/research/turbulence-intensity.md).

### Two stages of CFD

* **The screen:** all eight sections at the 20 points that can reject one (1, 3 and 5 knots at 0-8°,
  15 knots at 0° and 2°), at Tu inputs of 0.1 and 1\ %, either side of the calibrated bracket: 320
  cases. A section is rejected only if it loses at both inputs.
* **The finalists:** the survivors over all 57 points at Tu 0.3 and 0.6\ %: 342 cases. They decide
  the ranking.

## Results {#sec-results}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false}
**How the numbers are expressed.**

* **ΔD** = 100 × (candidate's board drag ÷ NACA 0006's − 1), at the same boat speed, side-force load,
  Tu input and rake. Positive means more drag (worse), negative less. These are board-drag
  percentages, not boat speed or race time.
* **Upwind** is the mean of ΔD over 5 speeds (1-5 knots) × 3 side-force loads, all 15 weighted
  equally: a mean of percentages, not a weighted race.
* **Downwind** is the mean of ΔD at 0°, zero side force, over the 9 speeds 1-15 knots, weighted
  equally: a sample of speeds, not every reaching angle or a continuous average.
* **Δ leeway** is the extra leeway the section needs for the same side force, in degrees.
:::

Click any chart to see it larger.

### The screen: eight sections {#sec-screen}

![The CFD screen: ΔD against NACA 0006. Upwind is the mean over 1, 3 and 5 knots and the three loads;
downwind is 0° at 1, 3, 5 and 15 knots. Pale hatched bars: Tu 0.1\ % (too laminar); solid: Tu 1\ %
(the higher input). The plank's bars are cut off at 22\ %.](../_generated/thistle-screen.svg){#fig-screen width="560px"}

![The same as a trade-off: upwind against downwind. Down and to the left is better both ways. At
Tu 0.1\ % nothing beats NACA 0006 upwind; at Tu 1\ % the 6-series are level upwind and 10-11\ % better
downwind.](../_generated/thistle-tradeoff.svg){#fig-tradeoff width="560px"}

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-screen}
{{< include ../_generated/thistle-screen.md >}}

ΔD against NACA 0006, %, rake 10° (negative = less drag). Upwind 1, 3 and 5 knots; downwind 1, 3, 5 and
15 knots. Stall margin in degrees past the high load, on a 2° grid, at Tu 0.1 / 1\ %: indicative only.
:::

* **The two parallel-sided boards lose at both inputs** and are rejected. The plank has 35-63\ % more
  drag upwind and 45-76\ % more downwind. The best parallel-sided board has 4-14\ % more upwind; it
  loses 12\ % downwind at Tu 0.1\ % and breaks even at 1\ %. Every step towards a foil helps, as
  Saporito et al. [-@saporito2020] found: a parallel-sided board at best matches a NACA section.
* **HT35 and SD8020 match NACA 0006** within the mesh resolution at both inputs, never ahead by more.
  NACA 0006-64 trades less than the 6-series. These three were dropped.
* **The two inputs disagree about the 6-series:** 10-12\ % behind upwind at Tu 0.1\ %, level at 1\ %,
  where they are 10-11\ % ahead downwind. So NACA 0006, 63-006 and 64-006 went on to the finalists.

### The finalists at the calibrated inputs {#sec-finalists}

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-results}
{{< include ../_generated/thistle-results.md >}}

The main answer: the finalists against NACA 0006 (ΔD, %; Δ leeway, degrees), rake 10°. Upwind: the
mean over 1-5 knots and the three side-force loads; downwind: 0° over the speeds shown.
:::

* **At Tu 0.3\ % NACA 0006 is clearly ahead upwind:** the 6-series have 9-11\ % more drag, well beyond
  the mesh resolution. They lose 12-13\ % at the working load and 13-16\ % at the high load, and only
  3\ % at the low load. NACA 0006 is ahead at 13 and 14 of the 15 speed and load points.
* **At Tu 0.6\ % it is a numerical near-tie on the mean:** +2.3 and +2.9\ %, inside the mesh
  resolution, and +1.0 and +0.4\ % at the working load. The 6-series are ahead at the low load (4-5\ %)
  and at 4-5 knots. NACA 0006's lead there rests on the **high load**, where the 6-series have 10-14\ %
  more drag, beyond the resolution.
* **Leeway:** the 6-series need about 0.1° more leeway for the same side force.
* **Downwind they have 5-8\ % less drag,** almost all of it at high speed: from 10 knots at Tu 0.3\ %,
  from 7.5 knots at 0.6\ %. At 4-5 knots they have more.
* **No stall veto was triggered.** The computed margins are at least 3.9° past the high load, but they
  rest on unconverged 8-10° solutions: indicative values, not a validated safety margin.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

**By the agreed rule** (upwind first; within ±1\ %, downwind decides), NACA 0006 is picked in 5 of the
6 cases of two Tu inputs × three rakes (@sec-rake). That count is the nominal outcome of the rule on
the same simulations, not six independent confirmations, and at Tu 0.6\ % the margins it compares are
smaller than the mesh resolution.

### How much the turbulence input decides it {#sec-turbulence}

![The 6-series against NACA 0006 at all four Tu inputs simulated, on the screen's speeds. The pink band
is the calibrated input bracket; the grey band the ±3\ % mesh resolution.](../_generated/thistle-bounds.svg){#fig-bounds width="560px"}

The upwind gap closes steadily as the input rises: 10-12\ % at Tu 0.1\ %, 8-9\ % at 0.3\ %, 1-2\ % at
0.6\ % and level at 1\ % (on the screen's 1, 3 and 5 knots). At 0.3\ % and 3 knots, NACA 0006's
suction side stays laminar much longer than the 6-series' at the working angle (@sec-why); at 0.6\ %
it turns turbulent earlier. The boundary layers at 1\ % were not examined, so the page does not
attribute the 6-series' downwind advantage there to a particular mechanism.

### The rake {#sec-rake}

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-rake}
{{< include ../_generated/thistle-rake.md >}}

The finalists' ΔD against NACA 0006, %, at rake 5°, 10° and 15°, upwind ("up") and downwind ("down").
The loads are held at the rake-10° values in newtons.
:::

More rake widens NACA 0006's lead upwind: at a given side force the section must work at a higher lift
coefficient. Only at Tu 0.6\ % with 5° rake are the 6-series within 1\ % upwind, so the rule hands the
decision to downwind there, for 64-006 (7.9\ % less drag).

### Checking against the measurements {#sec-check}

Is NACA 0006's upwind lead an artefact of the model? Two checks are consistent with it; neither
proves it.

![What the wind tunnel measured: drag against lift of NACA 0006 and 64-006 at Re 3 million (Report 824,
true 6\ % sections), with the percentage difference at three lift coefficients. 64-006 has less drag
only up to $C_l$ about 0.13; the Thistle's upwind side-force loads need about 0.1-0.45.](../_generated/thistle-r824.svg){#fig-r824 width="560px"}

1. **The measurements show the same trade.** At equal $C_l$, Report 824's 64-006 has 11\ % less drag
   than NACA 0006 at $C_l$ 0 and 8\ % less at 0.1, but 20\ % more at 0.2, 14\ % more at 0.3 and 8\ %
   more at 0.4. The upwind loads sit in the second range. But these are true 6\ % sections at Re
   3 million; the board works at 5.56\ % and, upwind, at Re 0.23-1.15 million.
2. **A sensitivity bracket for the model's bias.** The calibration matched the tunnel with NACA 0006 at
   an input of 0.3\ % and 64-006 at about 0.45\ %. Comparing them at those different inputs, 64-006 is
   still about 11\ % behind upwind (10.6-11.3\ %) and about level downwind (−5 to +5\ %). This is an
   illustration of how much the bias could matter, not a validated correction at the board's
   Reynolds numbers.

### Why NACA 0006 does better upwind {#sec-why}

![Three ways the water can run along the suction side (schematic, not computed): attached, laminar then
turbulent; a short laminar bubble that reattaches; and a long open separation near stall. Below each,
the sign of the skin friction $C_f$: negative where the flow next to the wall runs backwards.](../_generated/thistle-bl-schematic.svg){#fig-bl-schematic width="520px"}

![Computed, at 3 knots and 2° (about the working load) with Tu 0.3\ %: the shapes, the pressure on the
suction side and the skin friction. All three are at the **same angle**, so they make different lift:
this compares mechanisms, not equal side force. Markers: estimated transition (steepest rise of
$C_f$); shading: reversed wall friction (a short bubble).](../_generated/thistle-surface-tu03.svg){#fig-surface-03 width="560px"}

![The same at Tu 0.6\ %.](../_generated/thistle-surface-tu06.svg){#fig-surface-06 width="560px"}

* **Geometry to pressure.** The 6-series' sharper noses make a sharper suction peak right at the
  leading edge, and their pressure then rises (the curve falls) over the front, where NACA 0006's
  falls more gradually.
* **Pressure to friction, at Tu 0.3\ %.** NACA 0006's boundary layer stays laminar, with low friction,
  until the last few per cent of the chord (steepest friction rise at about 98\ %). On the 6-series it
  separates in a short bubble from about 74\ % to 79-81\ % of the chord and turns turbulent by about
  82\ %, with high friction over the rest. Their drag at 2° is 7\ % higher, and they make 11\ % less
  lift at that angle.
* **At Tu 0.6\ %** NACA 0006 turns turbulent at about 59\ % of the chord, the 6-series at about
  71-73\ %, with no bubble. Their drag at 2° is now lower, but NACA 0006 makes 10\ % more lift at the
  same angle, so at the same side force it is still about 4\ % ahead at 3 knots.

The 6-series' lower lift at the same angle is a model result that Report 824 doesn't show (it measured
similar lift slopes for both sections); the measured drag at equal $C_l$ (@fig-r824) points the same way
without it.

## The flow {#sec-flow}

**What these pictures are.** They illustrate the shape mechanisms behind the screen: NACA 0006 against
the two **rejected** parallel-sided boards, at 3 knots and the higher Tu input of 1\ %. They are not
visual evidence for the final NACA 0006 against 6-series ranking, which rests on the drag figures
above. Each frame is a separate steady solution at one angle (an angle sweep), not a time history.
The quantity, colour bar, flow direction, $C_l$, $C_d$ and convergence of every case are printed on the
frames.

::: {#fig-flow-sweep}
```{=html}
<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="../assets/thistle-flow-sweep-bl-poster.png" style="width:100%;height:auto;" aria-label="Angle sweep 0 to 8 degrees of NACA 0006, the parallel-sided board and the plank: signed streamwise velocity"><source src="../assets/thistle-flow-sweep-bl.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video>
```

Signed streamwise velocity along the suction side, 0-8°: NACA 0006 (top), parallel-l30-t50 (middle)
and the plank (bottom), 3 knots, Tu 1\ %. Blue is reversed flow, dark slow water, pale about the free
stream (the renderer's own colour bar is in the header). The poster shows the 8° frame.
:::

::: {#fig-flow-sweep-velocity}
```{=html}
<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="../assets/thistle-flow-sweep-velocity-poster.png" style="width:100%;height:auto;" aria-label="Angle sweep 0 to 8 degrees of the same three sections: flow speed magnitude"><source src="../assets/thistle-flow-sweep-velocity.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video>
```

The same cases as **flow speed** (magnitude, never negative) with streamlines: dark blue is slow water,
red faster than the boat. This map cannot show whether the flow is reversed. The renderer's own colour
bar is at the right; the renderer lit this view, so the field looks darker than the bar.
:::

![4°, signed streamwise velocity: mostly attached on all three. NACA 0006 and the parallel-sided board
have a tiny bubble at the nose (about 0.5-2\ % of the chord), the plank a short one just behind its
round nose (about 2-4\ %).](../assets/thistle-flow-4deg.png){#fig-flow-4}

![8°, signed streamwise velocity. NACA 0006 and the parallel-sided board did **not converge** at this
angle (marked on the frames): illustrative only. Blue here is reversed flow.](../assets/thistle-flow-8deg.png){#fig-flow-8}

* **0-4°: mostly attached, except short bubbles.** The bubbles above close within a few per cent of
  the chord. The plank's thick nose and straight taper leave a thicker wake: at 0° it has 67\ % more
  drag than NACA 0006 ($C_d$ 0.0105 against 0.0063). At 4° it makes 15\ % less lift for about the same
  drag, so it needs more angle, and more drag, for the same side force.
* **A short bubble against a long open separation.** A short bubble reattaches and costs little. At
  8° NACA 0006's reversed wall friction runs from the nose to about 22\ % of the chord ($C_l$ 0.71,
  $C_d$ 0.040), and the parallel-sided board's to about 80\ %, an open separation over most of the chord
  ($C_l$ 0.63, $C_d$ 0.068); both extents are from the surface friction data. These two solutions
  oscillate and did not converge, so they show where the separation sat in the solver's last
  iterations, not how it moves: dynamic stall or vortex shedding cannot be read from them.
* **The plank keeps its flow attached at 8°** behind its round nose: reversed friction only from about
  1 to 3\ % of the chord ($C_l$ 0.73, $C_d$ 0.015). But the high upwind load is at 4°, and its drag at the
  working loads is what loses.
* **At this speed and input the parallel-sided board is close to NACA 0006** below 6°: 1-2\ % more drag
  upwind, 13\ % less at 0°. It loses at the lower input (Tu 0.1\ %: 6-31\ % more upwind at 3 knots, 23\ %
  more at 0°), and its flow separates first as the angle rises.

**Pictures of the finalists** would need the flow fields of two existing cases, NACA 0006 and 64-006 at
3 knots, 2° and Tu 0.3\ % (@fig-surface-03). They were not downloaded for this page.

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

*Everything here comes from 2D simulations of the board's section, not from tests of a board.*

**Recommended reference section: NACA 0006 at 1 in** (5.56\ % of the 18 in chord), accepted for the
study on 25 October 2026. Before building any board, check with a class measurer whether the Official
Plans fix the section.

* **Among the eight sections simulated, it has the least upwind drag** at the calibrated Tu inputs.
  The evidence is strongest at Tu 0.3\ %: the 6-series have 9-11\ % more drag, and 12-16\ % at the
  working and high loads. NACA's own measurements show the same trade at Re 3 million.
* **At Tu 0.6\ % it is a numerical near-tie** on the mean (+2-3\ %, inside the mesh resolution; +0.4 and
  +1.0\ % at the working load). Its lead there rests on the high load, where the 6-series have 10-14\ %
  more drag.
* **The pre-agreed rule picks it in 5 of 6** Tu-input and rake cases: a nominal rule outcome on the same
  simulations, not six independent confirmations.
* **No stall veto was triggered** by the computed margins (at least 3.9°), which rest on unconverged
  solutions: not a validated safety margin.
* **Parallel-sided boards lose both ways.** A typical home-built plank has 35-63\ % more drag
  upwind. If a board is being rebuilt anyway, fairing it to a foil section matters more than the
  choice between foil sections.

**When a 6-series board might pay.** At the higher input of 1\ %, NACA 63-006 and 64-006 are level
upwind and 10-11\ % better downwind. And a sailor who cares more about the legs above 7.5 knots than
about upwind gets 10-17\ % less drag there for 2-11\ % more upwind. Neither was the agreed priority.

**Confidence: a model-dependent recommendation.** Strong enough to choose a reference section; not a
proof that no foil could do better. Why not more:

* **The model.** The turbulence input was calibrated at one Reynolds number (3 million) on two true 6\ %
  sections; 63-006 was not calibrated. Between sections its error differs by 10-20\ %, the size of the
  downwind differences.
* **The input is not the water.** The answer moves with the Tu input, and how a lake's turbulence,
  a board's roughness and waves map onto that input is not known.
* **The steady solver.** About a third of NACA 0006's points near 0-3° oscillate a little (drag
  varying by 2-8\ %). Its lead at the low load is within that; at the high load it is not. All 8-10°
  points are unsteady.
* **Assumed geometry.** The rake (10°, checked 5-15°), the 1.24 m of board below the hull and the span
  efficiency are assumptions, and 2D leaves out the tip, the hull junction and the board's planform.
* **Scope.** Eight sections were simulated and three run in full; untested shapes could do differently.
  No speeds between 5 and 7.5 knots, where NACA 0006's drag at 0° jumps.

**What would change it:**

* the Official Plans fixing the section, which would settle it;
* a measurement on real boards: a towing test, or two boats side by side;
* a section designed for 1 in at these Reynolds numbers (an optimisation was set up, but its gain
  would likely be a few per cent, within the model's error, so it was not run; an estimate);
* 3D simulations of the whole board under the hull.

## How the work went {#sec-studies}

Each study has a dated entry in the
[findings log](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/projects/foil2d/findings/thistle-board.md).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The studies, one by one (click to open)

::: {#tbl-studies}
| when | study | question | answer |
|:----|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------|
| 22-23\ Oct | set-up | What do the rules allow, and what chord does the water see? | At most 1 in thick; the shape may be fixed by the Official Plans. No published rake: 10° assumed, 5-15° checked; simple sweep theory. |
| 23\ Oct | XFOIL screen: 26 sections, 144 parallel-sided shapes | Which sections are worth simulating? | Eight, from NACA 0006 to a typical plank. The 6-series trade upwind for downwind; parallel-sided boards lose. |
| 23\ Oct | mesh study: 96 cases | Which mesh? | Fine: within 2-3\ % of extra fine at most points. Differences under 3\ % are not resolved. |
| 23\ Oct | validation against Report 824: 28 cases | Does the model match NACA's wind-tunnel data? | Lift yes; drag too low at low lift at the tunnel's turbulence, too high fully turbulent. 64-006 stalls early in the model. |
| 24\ Oct | Tu calibration: 40 cases | Which turbulence input reproduces the tunnel? | 0.3\ % for NACA 0006, about 0.45\ % for 64-006: the model favours the 6-series by 10-20\ %. |
| 23-24\ Oct | CFD screen: 8 sections, 320 cases (312 finished) | Which sections can be rejected? | Both parallel-sided boards. HT35, SD8020 and 0006-64 dropped. The 6-series go on. |
| 24-25\ Oct | finalists: 3 sections, 342 cases | Which wins at the calibrated inputs? | NACA 0006 upwind: clearly at Tu 0.3\ %, a near-tie at 0.6\ %; the 6-series 5-8\ % better downwind. |
| 25\ Oct | decision | | NACA 0006 at 1 in, accepted as the reference. |

The studies.

## Reproducing this {.appendix .unnumbered}

Everything is in [the repository](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd): the simulation setup
(`projects/foil2d/`), every study file (`thistle-*.yaml`), the board's inputs
(`projects/foil2d/design/thistle.yaml`), the section coordinates (`geometry/foils/`), the ranking code
(`src/iomcfd/boardrank.py`), the method (`projects/foil2d/methodology-thistle.md`) and the findings
log with the numbers behind each conclusion. This page's charts are drawn from the small data files
below, which `iomcfd site export` copies out of the runs; the rankings are computed from them with the
same code (`boardrank.rank`) that produced the findings. The flow pictures are ParaView renders
(`iomcfd viz`) of the 18 cases fetched whole; `tools/stack_viz_video.py` stacks them with their labels
and the renderer's own colour bars. The code is under the
[MIT licence](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/LICENSE); the text, figures and data on this
page are under CC BY 4.0. The HT35 and SD8020 coordinates come from the UIUC Airfoil Coordinates
Database, which states no licence for them; the Report 824 data were digitised from the report.
